A rig does not keep the water out. That is the first thing a certified diver is taught and
the thing everyone else at Kestrel gets wrong: the vault is at the pressure of two hundred
metres of ice and water, and nothing a co-op this size can build will hold a cavity against
it. So the rig fills the diver instead. The loop runs fluid through the lungs, and the diver
takes a wet breath and goes on taking them, and the only thing between her and the brine is
temperature and a mouthpiece.

This is why the rig is fitted rather than issued, and why there are two of them at Kestrel
Deep and only one person left who can wear either. Perfluorocarbon tolerance is a surgery and
a long convalescence, and the register certifies it separately from the soak. A member
without the tolerance who puts on a rig does not drown gradually. The loop will not start
against an untreated lung, and if it is forced it takes the lining with it.

The rig is also why the vault work is scheduled in six-hour blocks that have nothing to do
with the work. The nine hours on the charge are the easy part. The soak on either side is the
part that costs.
